:::question
Quick review: a model gives logits [3, 1, 1]. Without computing anything, what does setting T = 0.01 do to the distribution, and why might you not want that for creative writing?
:::
It becomes basically one-hot on the first token, so sampling always picks the same thing. For writing you would get repetitive, boring text.

# 4.1 Attention: queries, keys, values

So far each token's vector only knows about itself. **Attention** lets a token pull in information from earlier tokens. Take "bank" in *the river bank*:

```viz tokens
{ tokens: ["the", "river", "bank"], keys: ["the", "river", "bank"],
  weights: { from: 2, to: [0.23, 0.56, 0.21] }, causal: true,
  caption: "\"bank\" attends mostly to \"river\"." }
```

Each token's vector x is multiplied by three learned matrices:
- {{the query|q}}: what this token is looking for,
- {{the key|k}}: how other tokens can find it,
- {{the value|v}}: what it hands over if chosen.

$$\k{s}{s_j} = \frac{\k{q}{q} \cdot \k{k}{k_j}}{\sqrt{d}} \qquad \k{a}{a_j} = \mathrm{softmax}_j(\k{s}{s_j}) \qquad \k{o}{o} = \sum_j \k{a}{a_j}\,\k{v}{v_j}$$

```viz matrix
{ name: "K", rows: [[0.2, 0.1, -0.3], [1.1, 0.9, 0.4], [0.3, -0.2, 0.8]],
  rowLabels: ["k_the", "k_river", "k_bank"], rowKeys: ["the k", "river k", "bank k"],
  colLabels: ["d1", "d2", "d3"], heat: true, digits: 1,
  caption: "One key per earlier token (d = 3)." }
```

```viz steps
{ steps: [
  { md: "Make the {{query|q}} for *bank*: $q = x_{bank} W_Q$", hl: ["q"] },
  { md: "Score it against every {{key|k}}: $s_j = q \\cdot k_j / \\sqrt{d}$", hl: ["k", "s"] },
  { md: "Softmax the scores into {{weights|a}} that sum to 1", hl: ["s", "a"] },
  { md: "Add up the {{values|v}}, weighted: that's the {{output|o}}", hl: ["a", "v", "o"] } ] }
```

:::details Why divide by √d?
A dot product of two random d-dim vectors grows like √d. Without the division, scores in big models would be huge, softmax would be nearly one-hot, and almost no gradient would flow through it. Dividing keeps scores in a range where softmax stays soft ([softmax refresher](msg:2026-01-05.10)).
:::

Each set of W_Q, W_K, W_V is one [attention head](term:attention head); see it on the [map](map:attention). Later we'll see why keys and values get stored in a [KV cache](term:KV cache).

:::question
Why do q and k come from **different** matrices, instead of just scoring x_bank · x_river directly?
:::

:::example
Tiny numbers, d = 3. The query for *bank* (it is "looking for a place-type word"):

```viz vector
{ name: "q_bank", values: [1.0, 0.8, 0.0], labels: ["d1", "d2", "d3"], key: "q", heat: true }
```

Dot it with each key from [the matrix above](msg:2026-01-06.5), divide by √3, softmax:

```viz bars
{ title: "attention weights from *bank*", items: [
    { label: "the", value: 0.23, key: "the" },
    { label: "river", value: 0.56, key: "river" },
    { label: "bank", value: 0.21, key: "bank" } ], format: "pct", sort: true }
```

So *bank*'s output is 56% river's value, plus a bit of the others.
:::
Because x has to be normalized first? Different matrices let the model scale things differently so the scores do not blow up.

note: confused with scaling; missed relevance vs similarity

text:
Not quite: scaling is the √d's job ([details box](msg:2026-01-06.5)). The real reason is that **relevance isn't similarity**. With raw x · x, a token would match best with tokens that *look like itself*. But "bank" wants to find "river", a different word. Separate W_Q and W_K let the model learn a question space and an answer space: q asks "is there a place word nearby?", and k advertises "I am a place word".

:::warn
x_bank · x_bank is usually the biggest raw dot product, so without separate matrices every token would mostly attend to itself.
:::

In the [example](msg:2026-01-06.7), q_bank was built to look for place words, not to look like *bank*.

:::question
Try again in one sentence: what does having separate W_Q and W_K allow that x · x can't?
:::
It lets a token search for something different from what it is itself, like bank asking for a place word instead of for other banks.

reason: explained relevance vs similarity after a correction

text:
Yes. One more piece for today: real models run many heads side by side. Each [attention head](term:attention head) has its own W_Q, W_K, W_V and its own small output (e.g. 128 numbers). The outputs of all heads are glued together and mixed back into the token's vector.

:::question
Why have 32 small heads instead of one big one with the same total size?
:::
No idea really. Maybe it is faster to compute?

Speed is about the same, so that's not it. The reason: one head produces **one** set of weights per token, one softmax, so it can only blend one kind of lookup. With many heads, one can track the previous word, another the subject of the sentence, another matching brackets, all at once.

:::recap
- Attention: q · k scores → softmax → weighted sum of v ([explained](msg:2026-01-06.5), [example](msg:2026-01-06.7)).
- Separate W_Q/W_K because relevance ≠ similarity ([correction](msg:2026-01-06.10)).
- Many heads = many lookups in parallel ([skill page](skill:4.2)).
:::
